newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan court sets deadline for Punjab vote.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan court sets deadline for Punjab vote.

text.p: Pakistan's Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that Punjab province's newly reinstated chief minister can have two more days to prove that he commands a majority in the 248-member provincial assembly.
The court in Islamabad said Manzoor Wattoo must take a confidence vote in the provincial assembly by Sunday. Wattoo had asked the Supreme Court for two months to muster a majority.
The court extended the deadline by just two days.

The political crisis in populous Punjab, which had come to a head before President Farooq Leghari sacked Benazir Bhutto on November 5, has complicated moves by the caretaker government that replaced her to dissolve all provincial assemblies.

Leghari dismissed the National Assembly (lower house) when he removed Bhutto on charges of corruption and misrule. Three out of four provincial assemblies were then dissolved on similar grounds, leaving only Punjab, the richest and most important.
Leghari set a general election for February 3. Provincial elections normally take place three days after national polls.
Wattoo, a one-time Bhutto ally, was ousted in September 1995 on her advice. The Lahore High Court reinstated him on November 3 and he was told to secure a confidence vote by Friday.
The court said that if he lost the vote, this would lead to the automatic restoration of departing chief minister Arif Nakai, whose party is allied to Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
It also took a written pledge from Wattoo that he would not use his powers to dissolve the assembly if reinstated.

PPP assembly members filed a no-confidence motion against Wattoo, due to be considered on Saturday. But lawyers for Nakai, opposing Wattoo's request for a two-month grace period, told the Supreme Court that the no-confidence motion would be withdrawn.
Nakai replaced Wattoo last year after he was suspended by Leghari, acting on Bhutto's mandatory advice, following a revolt by most ministers in the central province that borders India.
Wattoo is unlikely to win Sunday's confidence vote because the PPP remains hostile to him, while its main opponent, the Pakistan Muslim League, has said it will boycott the vote.
After that the provincial assembly's fate will rest with newly appointed provincial governor Tariq Rahim.

Leghari sacked former governor Raja Saroop Khan after getting rid of Bhutto. He then named the chief justice of the Lahore High Court as acting governor, but the judge refused to dissolve the assembly because any future legal challenge to the dissolution would come before his court.
"Soon after the confidence vote on Sunday, the governor is likely to dissolve the assembly," one analyst said.
